questions.question: How do try, except, else, and finally work in Python?
questions.title: Python try, except, else, and finally
questions.direct_answer: Python runs `try` first, a matching `except` after a failure, `else` after a successful try, and `finally` before leaving the statement.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the four clauses and their execution paths are understood precisely.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming that `else` runs after an exception is handled, or that `finally` handles errors.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Keep the protected suite narrow and separate recovery, success work, and cleanup.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Put only the operation that may fail inside `try`.
The first compatible `except` handles the raised exception.
`else` runs only when the `try` suite finishes without an exception.
`finally` runs on success, handled failure, unhandled failure, or return.
Use `finally` for necessary cleanup, and avoid returning from it.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`try`, `except`, `else`, and `finally` describe four parts of one error-handling flow. The `try` suite contains the operation that is expected to fail in a known way. If it raises an exception, Python looks through the `except` clauses from top to bottom and runs the first handler whose type matches. If the `try` suite finishes normally, Python skips every handler and runs `else` instead. `finally` is the cleanup step and runs before control leaves the statement, whichever path was taken.

For example, when a program converts a configuration value to an integer, `int(text)` belongs in `try`. A `ValueError` handler can provide a clear configuration error. Starting the service belongs in `else`, because it should happen only after conversion succeeds and an error raised while starting should not be mistaken for a conversion error. Closing a separately acquired resource could belong in `finally`.

The `try` suite should be narrow. A wide block may catch a `ValueError` raised by unrelated code and handle the wrong problem. `finally` is also not a place for normal results: a `return` there can replace an earlier return or hide an active exception. For resources such as files, `with` is usually clearer than manual cleanup. In short, handlers recover from expected failures, `else` holds the success path, and `finally` guarantees essential cleanup.

sections.title: The four paths through try, except, else, and finally
sections.content:
An exception interrupts the remaining statements in the current suite. Python does not return to the line after the failure. It searches for a matching handler; after that handler finishes, execution continues after the complete `try` statement. If no handler matches, the exception keeps moving outward, but the local `finally` suite still gets its turn first.

`else` keeps the protected region precise. Suppose opening a file may raise `OSError`, while parsing its contents may raise `ValueError`. Protecting only `open()` and parsing in `else` prevents the file handler from claiming that malformed content was an open failure. This separation makes both the code and traceback more honest.

Cleanup must not depend on whether recovery succeeded. That is why `finally` is useful for manually acquired locks or temporary state. An exception raised inside `finally`, or a control statement such as `return`, can replace the result already in flight, so cleanup code should be short and predictable.

sections.title: Execution paths
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Enter try] --> B{Exception raised?}
  B -->|No| C[Run else]
  B -->|Yes| D{Matching except?}
  D -->|Yes| E[Run that handler]
  D -->|No| F[Keep exception active]
  C --> G[Run finally]
  E --> G
  F --> G
  G --> H{Exception still active?}
  H -->|No| I[Continue after try]
  H -->|Yes| J[Propagate to caller]
```

sections.title: Trace success, handled failure, and cleanup
sections.content:
```python
def parse_port(raw):
    events = []
    try:
        events.append("try")
        port = int(raw)
    except ValueError:
        events.append("except")
        return None, events
    else:
        events.append("else")
        return port, events
    finally:
        events.append("finally")

assert parse_port("8080") == (8080, ["try", "else", "finally"])
assert parse_port("http") == (None, ["try", "except", "finally"])
```

questions.question: How should multiple exception types be handled in Python?
questions.title: Handling Multiple Python Exceptions
questions.direct_answer: Use separate `except` clauses when recovery differs, a tuple when recovery is identical, and order related types from the most specific to the broadest.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether handlers are grouped by meaningful recovery rather than convenience.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting a broad parent handler first and making specific handlers ineffective.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect exception type, handler order, and the action this layer can complete.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use one handler per exception type when each failure needs different recovery.
Use `except (TypeError, ValueError)` when the same action is correct for both.
Python runs only the first compatible handler.
Place child exception classes before their parent classes.
Do not catch an exception unless this layer can handle or translate it.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Python can handle different failures with multiple `except` clauses. Each clause describes a type and the recovery that is correct for that type. Python checks them in source order and executes only the first compatible clause, so a specific subclass must appear before a broader parent. When two unrelated exceptions genuinely have the same response, their types can be placed in a tuple.

For example, loading a numeric setting can fail with `FileNotFoundError` if the file is absent, `PermissionError` if it cannot be opened, or `ValueError` if the text is not a number. Those cases normally deserve different messages. By contrast, if both `TypeError` and `ValueError` mean that an API argument is invalid, `except (TypeError, ValueError)` can share one boundary response.

A final `except Exception` may be useful at an application boundary that logs and translates unexpected operational failures, but silently continuing is unsafe. System-exiting exceptions such as `KeyboardInterrupt` are outside `Exception`, which is intentional. The practical rule is to group failures by recovery, keep handlers specific, and allow unknown failures to remain visible.

sections.title: Matching is based on class inheritance
sections.content:
An `except ParentError` clause also matches instances of every subclass of `ParentError`. That is useful when a family of errors shares a policy, but it creates an ordering rule: a parent placed first makes later child handlers unreachable for those values.

A tuple does not create a new hierarchy. It simply asks whether the raised object is an instance of any listed class. Use it only when the handler can perform the same complete action for each member. If one case should retry and another should report bad input, keep them separate.

The variable after `as` is the actual exception object. It carries the message and sometimes structured fields, such as `FileNotFoundError.filename`. That information can support a useful message without parsing the text of the exception.

sections.title: Choose the handler shape by recovery
sections.content:
| Situation | Form | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Different recovery | Separate `except` clauses | Each failure gets its own action |
| Same recovery | `except (A, B)` | Avoid duplicate handler code |
| Related parent and child | Child before parent | First compatible clause wins |
| Unknown failure | Let it propagate or translate at a boundary | Preserve evidence instead of hiding a bug |

sections.title: Give each file failure an honest result
